content: Topiramate is a relatively newer antiepileptic drug with a broad spectrum of activity. Some studies have suggested that it may be beneficial in treating juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME). However, there are currently no systematic reviews that definitively assess its efficacy and tolerability in this specific population. This review is an update of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2015 and last updated in 2019. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of topiramate in the treatment of JME. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted on August 26, 2021, using the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE. The CRS Web includes randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from multiple sources, including PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared topiramate to either placebo or other antiepileptic drugs in individuals with JME. The primary outcomes assessed were the proportion of participants achieving a significant reduction in seizures and the proportion experiencing adverse events (AEs). Two independent reviewers screened the identified studies, selected those meeting the inclusion criteria, extracted data, and assessed the methodological quality of the studies. Three studies involving a total of 83 participants were included in the analysis. In terms of efficacy, one study with 22 participants showed that a greater proportion of individuals in the topiramate group achieved a 50% or greater reduction in primarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures (PGTCS) compared to the placebo group (relative risk [RR] 4.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08 to 14.75). However, the certainty of this evidence was rated as very low. There were no significant differences between topiramate and valproate in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in myoclonic seizures (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.15; one study, 23 participants) or PGTCS (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.68 to 2.21; one study, 16 participants). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the proportion of participants becoming seizure-free (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.11; one study, 27 participants). The certainty of evidence for all these outcomes was rated as very low. Regarding tolerability, adverse events associated with topiramate were generally ranked as moderate to severe. In contrast, 59% of adverse events linked to valproate were classified as severe. Additionally, systemic toxicity scores were higher in the valproate group compared to the topiramate group. These findings were based on two studies involving 61 participants, and the certainty of evidence was again rated as very low. The included studies were judged to have a high risk of attrition bias and an unclear risk of reporting bias. For other domains, such as selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, and other biases, the risk was judged to be low to unclear. Overall, the certainty of the evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low using the GRADE approach. No new studies have been identified since the last version of this review in 2019. The current evidence does not provide sufficient support for the use of topiramate in the treatment of JME. While topiramate appears to be better tolerated than valproate, it does not demonstrate clear advantages over valproate in terms of efficacy. Further well-designed, double-blind RCTs with larger sample sizes are needed to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of topiramate in individuals with JME.
